title: Finding Slow Queries: pg_stat_statements, EXPLAIN, and Sizes
intro: Database CPU has crept up to 85% over a month. Nothing is broken, so pg_stat_activity shows nothing dramatic. You need history: which queries cost the most in total? Commands run from the shell with psql -c against the shop database.

steps.prompt: The pg_stat_statements extension records every kind of query the server runs. Show the 5 with the highest total execution time: select calls, mean_exec_time, total_exec_time, and query, ordered by total_exec_time descending.
expected_commands: psql -c "SELECT calls, mean_exec_time, total_exec_time, query FROM pg_stat_statements ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 5;"
psql -c "SELECT calls, mean_exec_time, total_exec_time, query FROM pg_stat_statements ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 5"
steps.fake_output:
calls   | mean_exec_time | total_exec_time |                        query
----------+----------------+-----------------+-----------------------------------------------------
 41200310 |           2.10 |     86520651.00 | SELECT * FROM products WHERE lower(sku) = $1
     1104 |       21044.80 |     23233459.20 | SELECT ... FROM orders JOIN order_items ... (report)
  9120044 |           0.31 |      2827213.64 | SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id = $1
   880312 |           1.90 |      1672592.80 | INSERT INTO orders ...
    42001 |          22.75 |       955522.75 | UPDATE products SET stock = stock - $1 WHERE id = $2
steps.hint: SELECT calls, mean_exec_time, total_exec_time, query FROM pg_stat_statements ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 5;
steps.explanation: The top query takes only 2 ms, but it ran 41 million times. The 21-second report is second.
steps.why: Order by total time, not mean time. The slow-query log would only ever show you the 21-second report; the real cost is a 2 ms query called constantly. A fast query run millions of times is the usual cause of creeping CPU, and the usual fix is an index or a cache, not hardware.

steps.prompt: Look at how the top query is executed, with real timings and buffer counts: run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on SELECT * FROM products WHERE lower(sku) = 'ab-1001'.
expected_commands: psql -c "EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM products WHERE lower(sku) = 'ab-1001';"
psql -c "EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM products WHERE lower(sku) = 'ab-1001'"
steps.fake_output:
Seq Scan on products  (cost=0.00..4310.00 rows=1 width=212) (actual time=1.204..2.091 rows=1 loops=1)
   Filter: (lower(sku) = 'ab-1001'::text)
   Rows Removed by Filter: 119999
   Buffers: shared hit=2810
 Planning Time: 0.080 ms
 Execution Time: 2.110 ms
steps.explanation: A sequential scan: it read all 120,000 rows and threw away all but one.
steps.why: There's an index on sku, but the query filters on lower(sku), and an index on a column can't serve a function of that column. 'Rows Removed by Filter' is the tell: work done and discarded. BUFFERS shows the I/O: 2,810 pages read for one row. Remember that EXPLAIN ANALYZE really runs the statement, so wrap a write in BEGIN ... ROLLBACK.

steps.prompt: Create an index that matches the expression, without blocking writes to the table: name it idx_products_sku_lower, on products (lower(sku)).
expected_commands: psql -c "CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_products_sku_lower ON products (lower(sku));"
psql -c "CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_products_sku_lower ON products (lower(sku))"
steps.explanation: An expression index on lower(sku). The same query now uses an index scan and takes about 0.03 ms.
steps.why: Plain CREATE INDEX blocks every write to the table until it finishes. CONCURRENTLY builds it while writes continue, at the price of taking longer, and it can't run inside a transaction. If it fails, it leaves an INVALID index behind that you must drop. Check with '\d products'.

steps.prompt: Indexes aren't free: each one slows every write and takes disk. Find indexes that have never been used: select indexrelname and idx_scan from pg_stat_user_indexes where idx_scan = 0.
expected_commands: psql -c "SELECT indexrelname, idx_scan FROM pg_stat_user_indexes WHERE idx_scan = 0;"
psql -c "SELECT indexrelname, idx_scan FROM pg_stat_user_indexes WHERE idx_scan = 0"
steps.explanation: Two indexes have had no scans since statistics were last reset.
steps.why: An unused index is pure cost. Before dropping one, check three things: how long ago the statistics were reset (a monthly report may not have run yet), that it isn't enforcing a unique constraint, and the replicas, which keep their own counters and may be where the reads go.

steps.prompt: See where the disk space goes. List the 5 largest tables including their indexes: select relname and pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(relid)) from pg_stat_user_tables, ordered by pg_total_relation_size(relid) descending.
expected_commands: psql -c "SELECT relname, pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(relid)) FROM pg_stat_user_tables ORDER BY pg_total_relation_size(relid) DESC LIMIT 5;"
psql -c "SELECT relname, pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(relid)) FROM pg_stat_user_tables ORDER BY pg_total_relation_size(relid) DESC LIMIT 5"
steps.fake_output:
relname   | pg_size_pretty
-------------+----------------
 audit_log   | 212 GB
 orders      | 41 GB
 order_items | 38 GB
 sessions    | 9120 MB
 products    | 310 MB
steps.hint: SELECT relname, pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(relid)) FROM pg_stat_user_tables ORDER BY pg_total_relation_size(relid) DESC LIMIT 5;
steps.explanation: An audit log nobody queries is five times the size of the orders table.
steps.why: pg_total_relation_size includes indexes and large-value storage; pg_relation_size is the table alone. Append-only tables such as audit logs and sessions grow for ever unless something removes old rows. The clean answer is partitioning by time, so an old month is dropped as a whole partition instead of deleted row by row.

steps.prompt: Log every statement slower than 500 ms from now on, so the next slow query leaves a trace. Set log_min_duration_statement server-wide.
steps.explanation: After a reload, statements over 500 ms are written to the server log with their duration.
steps.why: The slow log and pg_stat_statements answer different questions: the log gives individual slow executions with their parameters and timestamps; the extension gives totals without parameters. The auto_explain module goes further and logs the plan of each slow statement, which is the only way to catch a query that's slow only sometimes.
